title: Anisotropic hydrogen embrittlement behavior of hot-rolled A572 steel
abstract: Abstract In the present work, an investigation of the susceptibility to hydrogen embrittlement of a hot rolled ASTM A572 steel with a banded pearlite/ferrite microstructure was conducted, with the objective of elucidating the anisotropic mechanical behavior of the steel when submitted to hydrogen charging. To this end, tensile test samples were prepared with the tensile axis oriented parallel and perpendicular to the rolling direction of 5.0 mm thick sheets. Hydrogen charging was performed by cathodic polarization. Then, ex-situ tensile tests were carried out on both pristine and exposed samples. Using this methodology, it was possible to verify that the ASTM A572 steel is more susceptible to hydrogen embrittlement when the tensile axis is perpendicular to the rolling direction, and that the influence of prior hydrogen charging is significantly higher after necking. By analyzing the microstructure of specimens submitted to interrupted tensile tests, heterogenous strain partitioning between ferrite and pearlite was identified, which led to crack initiation and development along ferrite/pearlite interfaces. It was possible to show that fracture is facilitated when the main crack front is aligned with pearlite bands, resulting in a greater hydrogen-induced ductility loss.

sections.heading: Introduction
paragraphs: One of the current global challenges found in sustainable energy production is the development of safe and reliable storage mechanisms, considering the intrinsically intermittent nature of power generation by common renewable sources like solar and wind. The emergence of energy carriers such as hydrogen has gained prominence in the last decades, even with the vision of a “hydrogen economy” 1 , because of the possibility of obtaining hydrogen gas from the electrolysis of water powered by renewable energy resources—“green hydrogen”—that can later be used for power generation, producing clean emissions. The widespread incorporation of hydrogen as a clean energy carrier, however, depends on important advances in the areas of hydrogen generation, storage and distribution 2 . From a structural integrity perspective, disposing of hydrogen in metallic vessels can be challenging because of hydrogen embrittlement: the degradation of mechanical properties, usually in the form of a loss in ductility or strength, observed in metals exposed to hydrogen 3 , which is also seen in the context of natural gas pipelines 4 .

Different mechanisms have been reported by which hydrogen may deteriorate mechanical properties of structural materials, such as hydrogen enhanced decohesion (HEDE), hydrogen enhanced local plasticity (HELP), adsorption induced-dislocation emission (AIDE), hydride formation, among others 3 , 5 . However, common steps in all cases involve hydrogen adsorption at the metal surface and trapping in its interior at different sites (reversible or irreversible). Hydrogen trapped at reversible sites is mobile and can be considered more detrimental to mechanical properties due to its ability to move to highly stressed regions in the material  e.g . crack tips 6 . In the case of general carbon and/or low alloys steels, trapping sites are diverse and may include grain boundaries, carbide/matrix interfaces, dislocations, among other microstructural features that may be classified as reversible or irreversible 7 , 8 .

In this context, it is important to consider the interaction of absorbed hydrogen with the material’s particular microstructure and previous processing when analyzing its susceptibility to embrittlement, particularly in the case of ferrous alloys, which are known to exhibit a multitude of microstructure and property combinations 9 . Pearlite colonies and cementite lamellae can influence hydrogen uptake, trapping and transport in steels. Ferrite/cementite interfaces may act as hydrogen trapping sites, while the lamellar structure of pearlite can modify hydrogen diffusion paths and contribute to anisotropic hydrogen transport depending on its orientation within the microstructure 10 ,  11 ,  12 – 13  consequently modifying the steels susceptibility to embrittlement. For instance, it has been shown recently that in cold-drawn pearlitic steel wires submitted to hydrogen charging during mechanical loading, crack initiation and propagation is preferentially observed at the cementite/ferrite interfaces found in pearlite 14 , 15 , which led to an improvement in hydrogen embrittlement resistance along the drawing direction. An anisotropic behavior in mechanical properties was also observed in a X65 pipeline steel subject to hydrogen charging, which exhibited fracture toughness values approximately 60% lower in the longitudinal and transversal pipe directions compared to the radial direction 16 , and was found to be more susceptible to the influence of hydrogen when submitted to tensile loading perpendicular to the rolling direction, compared to loading parallel to the rolling direction 17 .

Based on these premises, in this work, a study of the susceptibility to hydrogen embrittlement of an ASTM A572 grade 50 high strength low alloy steel, obtained in the hot rolled condition, is presented. Because of the hot rolling process in which it is frequently supplied, the A572 steel exhibits a typical banded structure composed of ferrite grains and pearlite colonies, thus creating the possibility of analyzing the influence of hydrogen on mechanical behavior along different directions. The study is relevant due to the widespread use of the A572 steel in various structural applications, including pressure vessels and pipelines in which the material might be subject to complex loads, involving triaxial stress states that could lead to anisotropic mechanical behavior and eventually unexpected failure. The main contribution of the present work is the establishment of the microstructural origins of anisotropic hydrogen embrittlement of a commercially important steel by taking into consideration ferrite/pearlite band orientation, hydrogen-induced interface damage as well as crack initiation mechanisms.

sections.heading: Uninterrupted tensile tests
paragraphs: In order to assess the influence of hydrogen on the A572 steel’s microstructure and properties, tensile test specimens with the tensile axis aligned with the rolling direction (longitudinal loading) and with the transversal direction (transversal loading) were submitted to hydrogen charging and subsequently tested. Representative stress-strain diagrams obtained from the tensile tests performed on pristine and hydrogen-charged samples submitted to longitudinal loading are presented in Fig.  1(a, b) , while those submitted to transversal loading are presented in Fig.  1(c, d ). In Fig.  1(a, c ) the actual stress-strain (σ-ε) diagrams are shown, whereas in Fig.  1(b, d ), instantaneous strain-hardening (dσ/dε) plots are presented. The results obtained, before and after hydrogen charging, are summarized in Table  1 . The pristine A572 steel exhibited small differences in mechanical behavior depending on the loading direction. Although similar yield and tensile strength values were identified, the samples tested along the longitudinal direction exhibited lower ductility (and earlier necking, in terms of strain) compared to the samples loaded along the transversal direction, in agreement with a previous investigation 18 . Fig. 1 Results obtained from the tensile tests before and after hydrogen charging. a  Stress–strain diagrams parallel to loading direction (longitudinal loading),  b  instantaneous strain-hardening in longitudinal loading,  c  stress–strain diagrams perpendicular to loading direction (transversal loading) and  d  instantaneous strain-hardening in transversal loading. Table 1 Summary of the tensile tests results obtained before and after hydrogen charging (YS—Yield Strength, TS—Tensile Strength) Loading condition TS strain Fracture strain YS (MPa) TS (MPa) HEI HEI’ Longitudinal, no H 14.9 ± 0.8% 25.7 ± 2.4% 428 ± 10 551 ± 8 21.8% 50.0% Longitudinal, with H 14.7 ± 0.6% 20.1 ± 1.3% 428 ± 5 542 ± 2 Transversal, no H 14.7 ± 1.4% 22.5 ± 3.0% 441 ± 10 558 ± 13 25.1% 65.9% Transversal, with H 14.2 ± 1.6% 16.9 ± 0.6% 434 ± 6 544 ± 6

From the results presented in Fig.  1 , it is possible to notice that cathodic polarization in an acid solution led to a modification in the mechanical behavior of the tested steels, for the two loading directions considered. In both cases, after hydrogen charging, a loss in ductility could be observed (evaluated in terms of the relative maximum elongation, or the strain at fracture) with a slight reduction in the ultimate tensile strength values. In addition, specifically regarding the change in ductility, it is possible to notice that the influence of hydrogen was more significant after the point of necking, since both yield and tensile strength values (along with corresponding strain levels) remained practically unaltered for both loading directions, with and without charging. Furthermore, the instantaneous strain hardening plots also indicate similar deformation behavior among the tested samples, up to the point of necking, with only small differences in deformation behavior caused by hydrogen charging, and in fact similar strain values corresponding to the onset of necking, as reported in Table  1 . Therefore, although hydrogen charging may influence the deformation behavior during uniform plastic flow, its effects on the A572 steel specimens become more pronounced after the onset of necking, when deformation becomes inhomogeneous and microvoid formation is initiated, in agreement with previous research 14 , 19 , 20 .

Cathodic charging had a comparatively smaller influence on deformation prior to necking, although a slight modification in yielding can be observed in Fig.  1c , likely associated with hydrogen–dislocation interactions during plastic deformation. However, at the onset of necking, a triaxial stress state develops with a growing hydrostatic stress component. In the regions where an elevated tensile hydrostatic stress is found, hydrogen’s chemical potential is lowered 22 , increasing hydrogen concentration by lattice diffusion, which is then trapped at ferrite/pearlite interfaces causing local decohesion 23 ,  24 – 25 . It is worth considering that in perpendicular loading hydrogen diffusion along the material’s cross section is faster compared to parallel loading given the relative orientation of ferrite/pearlite bands and the tensile axis (hydrogen diffusivity is higher along the longitudinal direction relative to the transversal direction in steels with a banded structure 21 ), which could potentially increase the amount of trapped hydrogen at ferrite/pearlite boundaries, consistent with the tensile test results obtained after hydrogen charging.

Based on the data obtained from the tensile tests and considering that the influence of hydrogen charging was found to be more significant after the point of maximum load (non-uniform deformation), the relative embrittlement was determined by applying Eqs.  1  and  2  and the obtained values are indicated in Table  1 . It is possible to notice that the samples loaded along the longitudinal direction, which exhibited higher overall ductility, were found to be less susceptible to embrittlement considering both the relative change in overall elongation (HEI, Eq.  1 ) and the relative change in elongation in the range between necking and fracture (HEI’, Eq.  2 ). The result is in agreement with a previous investigation which showed that a X65 pipeline steel was more susceptible to hydrogen embrittlement when loading was performed perpendicular to the rolling direction 17 . The obtained values for the hydrogen embrittlement indices reflect the identified tendency, that the influence of hydrogen charging was more largely felt at higher levels of plastic deformation, particularly after the point of necking, given that for both cases HEI’ > HEI. This could be expected, since the presence of hydrogen is known to be less severe in more ductile materials, as the low carbon steel evaluated in the present work 26 .

The characteristics of the fracture surfaces observed by SEM after tensile testing are presented in Figs.  2  and  3 , for the samples loaded parallel and perpendicular to the rolling direction, respectively (all images were registered in secondary electron mode). In both cases, figs. (a-d) correspond to samples tested after hydrogen charging, while figs. (e, f) originate from samples tested without hydrogen charging. The reduction in ductility observed after charging was clearly reflected on the overall fracture surface, as can be seen by comparing Fig.  2(a, e)  and Fig.  2(a, e) . After hydrogen charging, the total cross-section area of the fractured specimens remained rectangular, indicating mostly uniform deformation (hence limited plastic deformation beyond necking), while in the pristine specimens the cross-section surface clearly experienced not only significant inhomogeneous deformation, but also higher levels of plastic deformation overall relative to the original 5 × 7 mm 2  cross-section. Fig. 2 Fracture surface of tensile test specimens loaded parallel to rolling direction. a  With H-charging, overview,  b  with H-charging, transition from outer ductile fracture to inner brittle fracture,  c  with H-charging, internal brittle fracture region,  d  with H-charging, ductile features in the outer portions of the cross-section,  e  without H-charging, overview and  f  without H-charging, ductile fracture morphology in the central region of the cross-section. Fig. 3 Fracture surface of tensile test specimens loaded perpendicular to the rolling direction. a  With H-charging, overview,  b  with H-charging, central region,  c  with H-charging, brittle features surrounding transversal cracks,  d  with H-charging, ductile fracture morphology identified in the outer portions of the specimen,  e  without H-charging, overview and  f  without H-charging, ductile features surrounding transversal cracks.

Concerning initially the case presented in Fig.  2(a) , it can be seen that the fracture surface of the hydrogen charged specimen is composed of an internal ellipse-shaped region with a distinct contrast relative to the remainder of the cross-section. The distinct regions were found to be associated with different fracture mechanisms. In the outer portions of the fractured specimen—upper part of Fig.  2(b) —fracture was found to be ductile, with mostly features indicating microvoid coalescence (MVC), as shown in Fig.  2(d) . In contrast, in the inner portion of the cross-section, corresponding to the lower portion of Fig.  2(b) , quasi-cleavage (QC) morphology was found to be dominant 27 , 28 , indicative of brittle fracture, as seen in Fig.  2(c) . These results are in agreement with previous reports, which also identified ductile fracture features on the periphery of tensile test steel specimens charged with hydrogen, along with brittle characteristics in the central region 19 , 29 . The findings also support the idea that in mixed fracture mode, brittle fracture is initiated in the central regions of the material (for example, near inclusions), propagating radially (hence the ellipse-shaped brittle region) towards the outer regions where MVC is dominant 3 . In contrast, the sample submitted to tensile testing without H-charging, examined in Fig.  2(e, f) , exhibited ductile fracture with the presence of MVC in the entire analyzed cross-section.

The results presented in Fig.  3  also reveal differences in fracture morphology upon loading perpendicular to rolling direction after hydrogen charging. The distinctive ellipse-shaped region seen in Fig.  2(a)  was not found with transversal loading, probably because of the lower amount of inhomogeneous deformation observed relative to the longitudinal loading condition (Fig.  1 ). The central region of the specimen cross-section also exhibited QC fracture modes, and ductile fracture was found only along the edges of the examined surface, as seen in Fig.  3 c, d, respectively. The significantly smaller area of ductile fracture found in perpendicular loading relative to parallel loading is consistent with the differences in hydrogen embrittlement susceptibility registered in Table  1 . For the samples tested without previous hydrogen charging, the fracture mechanisms were ductile overall, as seen in Fig.  3 e, f. The main difference relative to the samples loaded along the rolling direction is crack-growth direction. In Fig.  3(b) , the presence of a series of cracks developing along the transversal direction of the tested specimen, i.e. parallel to the rolling direction and perpendicular to the loading direction, can be clearly noticed (the underlying mechanism relative to crack formation is explored in the following section). Between these cracks, the fracture mode is brittle, dominated by QC, as seen in Fig.  3(c) . Similar cracks were also found in the pristine samples, Fig.  3(f) , but they were intermediated by ductile fracture characteristics. From a fracture mechanics perspective, this behavior can be explained by considering that microcracks that are transversal to the tensile axis are loaded predominantly in Mode-I and generate higher stress intensity values (K I ), with elevated hydrostatic stresses at the crack tip. As a consequence, hydrogen segregates to the crack tips, reducing interfacial cohesion and causing fracture with no significant subsequent plastic deformation, resulting in the QC features seen in the center of the fractured specimens.

sections.heading: Interrupted tensile tests
paragraphs: Since the influence of hydrogen on the mechanical properties of the A572 steel was found to be dependent on the loading direction relative to rolling, tensile tests interrupted slightly beyond the point of necking (between 3.4 and 5.1% engineering strain) were conducted on samples that were subsequently submitted to microscopic examination. The microstructure of hydrogen charged samples loaded parallel and perpendicular to the rolling direction is shown in Fig.  4(a-d) . In all cases, the observation plane corresponded to the rolling plane of the tensile specimens, i.e. the surface of the rolled sheets from which the specimens were obtained. For the sample loaded parallel to the rolling direction, the tensile test was interrupted at an engineering strain of 5.1% above the point of necking, while for the sample loaded perpendicular to the rolling direction the test was interrupted at an engineering strain of 3.4% past the point of necking. The difference occurred due to difficulties in determining the actual maximum load during testing, considering the stress “plateau” that can be seen in Fig.  1 . In Fig.  4(a, c) , microstructure overviews from the parallel and perpendicular loaded specimens are presented, respectively, with identification of cracks developed during tensile testing. The discontinuities were identified in micrographs obtained before etching with the 2% Nital solution, in which they could be readily discerned from the surrounding material, and the images were subsequently superimposed on images from the same samples after the microstructure was revealed. It can be seen that the cracks are oriented along the rolling direction of the tested specimens, regardless of the loading direction. Furthermore, the cracks are concentrated near the pearlite bands for both loading directions. A closer examination of selected cracks identified in Fig.  4(a, c)  is shown in Fig.  4(b, d) , revealing that the cracks develop along the ferrite/pearlite interfaces, similar to previous investigations 10 , 30 . The results presented in Fig.  4  are consistent with the observations of the fracture surface (Figs.  2  and  3 ), which showed the development of cracks along the transversal direction of the test specimens, in case of the specimens loaded perpendicular to the rolling direction. Fig. 4 Microstructure analysis from interrupted tensile tests after hydrogen charging. a  Longitudinal (parallel) loading overview,  b  crack development in parallel loading,  c  transversal (perpendicular) loading overview and  d  crack development in perpendicular loading.

The initiation and development of the cracks identified in Fig.  4 , predominantly at the pearlite/ferrite interfaces can be explained by considering the differences in mechanical properties between pearlite and ferrite, which lead to inhomogeneous strain partitioning in the material, along with the higher concentration of hydrogen in these regions, which constitute more favorable trapping sites 10 . Due to the dispersion of carbides in its interior, the pearlite colonies exhibit superior hardness and are more resistant to plastic deformation compared to the surrounding ferrite grains, causing strain incompatibility at their interface when the material is loaded in tension. This can be confirmed by analyzing the results presented in Fig.  5 , in which the distribution of ferrite grain and pearlite colony aspect ratios is shown, considering the different loading conditions investigated in the present work. In the as-received material (Fig.  8 ), the ratio between the maximum length of individual particles (either ferrite grains or pearlite colonies) exhibited a distribution centered around unity, meaning there was not a systematic deviation in terms of length or width in the microstructure constituents relative to the rolling direction of the A572 sheet. However, the same analysis performed on samples taken from interrupted tensile tests produced, as expected, a deviation in aspect ratio as shown in Fig.  5 . In all cases, the distribution center is greater than one, indicating a relative elongation of the microstructure constituents along the loading direction. Furthermore, it is possible to notice from the results presented in Fig.  5  that the deviation from unity is larger for the ferrite grains in comparison to the pearlite colonies, consistent with the higher mechanical strength of pearlite. Consequently, an incompatibility in deformation is observed across the ferrite/pearlite interfaces, which accumulate higher shear and normal stresses. These boundaries act as reversible traps 7 , so the amount of retained hydrogen changes as stresses are redistributed either by plastic deformation or crack initiation/development. In the presence of hydrogen, dislocation mobility in ferrite is enhanced (HELP) 31 , promoting further plastic deformation in this softer phase and increasing the strain mismatch with the surrounding pearlite. This process contributes to the formation of localization bands at ferrite/pearlite boundaries 32 . Simultaneously, stress-assisted diffusion drives hydrogen toward these highly stressed regions, increasing its local concentration at the interfaces. Under these conditions, the cohesive strength of the ferrite/pearlite boundaries may be reduced, facilitating interfacial decohesion (HEDE) and the nucleation of microcracks along the pearlite bands. Therefore, the present observations are consistent with a situation in which hydrogen-enhanced localized plasticity promotes stress localization, while hydrogen accumulation at the interfaces facilitates decohesion, resulting in a synergistic interaction between HELP and HEDE mechanisms 33 . Fig. 5 Normalized distribution of particle (ferrite grains or pearlite colonies) aspect ratio relative to loading direction from interrupted tensile tests. a  Longitudinal loading, without hydrogen charging,  b  longitudinal loading, after hydrogen charging,  c  transversal loading, without hydrogen charging and  d  transversal loading after hydrogen charging.

It is also interesting to notice that the relative size of the microcracks identified in Fig.  4  varies significantly when hydrogen charging is involved. Average crack length, relative area fraction and density were obtained from micrographs of samples submitted to interrupted tensile tests, and the data are compared in Fig.  6 . The average microcrack length values were calculated based on the average of the longest cracks found on each analyzed surface (a particle was considered as crack if the ratio between long and short axes was greater than 2.0, with a minimum length of 30 pixels or 0.064 mm). In Fig.  6 , the strain imposed until the tests were interrupted is presented relative to the point of necking (Δε), as well as the tensile toughness, U (determined by integration of the engineering stress-strain curves). The average microcrack length found in each situation was of 0.26 ± 0.07, 0.10 ± 0.04, 0.24 ± 0.07, and 0.11 ± 0.02 mm, respectively, for the samples submitted to longitudinal loading after hydrogen charging, longitudinal loading without hydrogen charging, transversal loading with hydrogen charging, and transversal loading without hydrogen charging. As such, the results indicate that hydrogen leads to a significant decrease in the accumulated strain energy required for the development of micro-cracks, for loading both parallel and perpendicular to the steel’s rolling direction. Fig. 6 Summary of average crack length found in interrupted tensile tests, along with corresponding deformation values (beyond necking, Δε) and tensile toughness (U).

As shown in Fig.  6 , the average microcrack length did not differ significantly between specimens loaded parallel and perpendicular to the rolling direction after hydrogen charging. However, additional image analysis performed on the interrupted tensile specimens revealed differences in the crack population between the two loading orientations. In particular, specimens subjected to longitudinal loading after hydrogen charging exhibited a higher crack density (0.65 cracks/mm²) compared to specimens loaded in the transversal direction (0.29 cracks/mm²). Despite this difference, the fraction of the analyzed area occupied by cracks was very similar in both cases (approximately 0.21%), indicating that the overall extent of crack development was comparable. These observations suggest that under transversal loading, fewer cracks accounted for a similar cracked area fraction, implying greater crack opening or development in the observation plane. This behavior is consistent with the orientation of the ferrite/pearlite interfacial cracks relative to the applied stress. In the case of transversal loading, the cracks are oriented approximately perpendicular to the tensile axis and therefore experience a more favorable Mode-I loading condition, which promotes crack opening and facilitates crack coalescence, leading to macroscopic fracture. Conversely, under longitudinal loading, the microcracks remain largely aligned with the tensile axis and are therefore less favorably oriented for crack opening. Consequently, a larger number of microcracks may form without contributing as effectively to the propagation of the main fracture. Naturally, in both cases, the main cracks associated with the final rupture develop perpendicular to the tensile axis, but the microcracks formed during earlier stages assist the fracture process 34 , 35  reducing overall ductility. Because of the steel’s banded structure, in the case of perpendicular loading, the initial microcracks that develop along ferrite/pearlite interfaces are parallel to the fracture surface, accelerating the fracture process and resulting in higher embrittlement levels compared to the samples submitted to longitudinal loading.

In conclusion, in the present work, the susceptibility to hydrogen embrittlement of a hot-rolled ASTM A572 steel, with a banded ferrite-pearlite microstructure, was evaluated by considering loading conditions relative to the materials original rolling direction. After hydrogen charging, loading both parallel and perpendicular to the rolling direction led to a loss in ductility and to the appearance of brittle characteristics in the fractured surfaces, but with significantly higher losses in ductility when the tensile axis was perpendicular to the rolling direction. The tensile tests performed with and without hydrogen charging showed that hydrogen had a stronger influence on mechanical behavior at the onset of necking when deformation becomes inhomogeneous, and a triaxial stress-state is formed. By analyzing the microstructure of specimens submitted to interrupted tensile tests, it was found that strain partitioning between ferrite and pearlite caused stress concentration at their boundaries, and the interfaces were found to be preferential crack initiation/development sites. Thus, specimens submitted to loading perpendicular to the rolling direction experienced crack propagation across the material’s natural fracture surface, which explains the greater loss in ductility experienced.

sections.heading: Materials
paragraphs: The material employed in the present investigation was an ASTM A572 grade 50 high strength low allow steel, obtained in the hot-rolled condition. The steel composition, determined by optical emission spectroscopy, consisted of 0.180%C, 0.350%Si, 1.510%Mn, 0.016%P, 0.008%S, 0.022%Al, 0.010%Cu, 0.014%Nb, 0.002%V, 0.014%Ti and balance Fe (values in weight %). The initial microstructure of the hot-rolled steel is presented in Fig.  7 , with an indication of the rolling direction. The microstructure is composed of banded pearlite colonies and ferrite grains, with an average ferrite grain size of 8.6 ± 3.2 μm. Tensile test specimens with a rectangular (5 × 7 mm) cross-section were prepared, with loading directions parallel and perpendicular to the original rolling direction of the metal plates. The total length of the tensile test specimens was 180 mm, with a gauge length of 50 mm. Fig. 7 Microstructure of the hot-rolled ASTM A572 grade 50 steel used in the present investigation (observation carried out on the sheet normal direction plane).

sections.heading: Hydrogen charging and tensile testing
paragraphs: The exposure to hydrogen was accomplished by cathodic charging of the tensile test specimens using a two-electrode electrochemical cell, with graphite rods as counter electrodes, in a 0.5 M H 2 SO 4  solution containing 0.25 g/l NaAsO 2  as a hydrogen recombination agent, as used in a previous investigation 36 . Because an acid solution was used, the specimens were weighed before and after charging to ensure that no dissolution took place upon exposure to the selected electrolyte. The gauge length of the specimens was covered with a chemically inert insulating tape, leaving an exposed area of 2.52 cm 2  situated at the center of the gauge length, and the cathodic charging was carried out at a current density of 30 mA/cm 2  for a duration of 24 hours. The gauge surfaces of the tensile specimens were left in the as-machined condition obtained by milling and were not polished. During charging, all faces of the test specimens were exposed to the solution during hydrogen charging. The charging parameters were selected based on the previous work of Brandolt and co-workers, who analyzed the influence of hydrogen charging on the mechanical behavior of a high strength steel by performing ex-situ tensile tests 37 . While these parameters can be considered relatively severe for steels (see e.g. refs.  38 , 39 ), they were selected in an attempt to promote a more uniform hydrogen distribution with the material’s cross-section. Electrochemical charging under acidic conditions and relatively high current densities can introduce substantial hydrogen concentrations in steels. Although some diffusible hydrogen may leave the material after removal from the electrolyte, a significant fraction remains temporarily trapped at microstructural defects and can therefore influence the mechanical response during short-duration mechanical testing 11 , 40 .

In order to follow the influence of hydrogen charging on the damage evolution during tensile testing, additional tests were performed and interrupted after the point of necking on both charged and non-charged specimens. In these experiments, the specimens were submitted to loading as in a conventional tensile test, but after necking the test was interrupted, the non-fractured specimens were unloaded and set aside for further examination. A reference of elongation after necking (Δε = 4%) was chosen arbitrarily but could not be achieved unambiguously due to the difficulty in determining the exact point of maximum load during tensile testing. As such, the actual values of Δε were 5.1%, 3.7%, 3.4% and 4.1% for the specimens submitted to longitudinal loading with charging, longitudinal without charging, transversal loading with charging and transversal loading without charging, respectively.

sections.heading: Characterization
paragraphs: The microstructure of the A572 steel samples submitted to interrupted tensile tests was analyzed by optical microscopy (OM) and scanning electron microscopy (SEM). The microscopy samples were cut from the tensile test specimens such that the loading and transversal directions were situated in the observation plane. Preparation involved conventional metallographic procedures of grinding and polishing down to a 1 µm finish in an Al 2 O 3  suspension, followed by etching in a 2% Nital solution. The OM analyses were performed with a Zeiss Axio A.1 microscope, while the SEM observations were carried out in a JEOL JSM IT300 microscope. Quantitative analyses were carried out in order to extract information from individual ferrite grains and pearlite colonies. The procedures were performed using WEKA segmentation 41  associated with the FIJI distribution of ImageJ software (open source) 42 , because of its widespread availability and its proven application in quantitative microstructure analyses 43 . The procedure is illustrated in Fig.  8 a, b which depict the original microstructure (as observed by OM after 2% Nital etching) and the classified image highlighting ferrite and pearlite particles, respectively. The quantitative analysis was performed mostly with the objective of assessing the aspect ratio distribution of ferrite grains and pearlite colonies, as illustrated in Fig.  8(c) , which was obtained from the as-received A572 steel. The ratio between the length of each individual constituent along the rolling direction (RD) and transversal direction (TD) was evaluated, and the normalized frequency was plotted accordingly. For the case shown in Fig.  2(c) , a total of 2133 ferrite and 559 pearlite particles were evaluated and for both cases the center of the distribution is close to unity (1.042 and 0.998, for ferrite and pearlite, respectively), which means that despite the banded structure seen in Fig.  7 , the individual grains/colonies are not significantly elongated or distorted along a particular direction. Fig. 8 Quantitative microscopy analysis performed with assistance of WEKA segmentation. a  Microstructure of the as-received material revealed by OM,  b  classified image showing ferrite and pearlite particles and  c  normalized histogram showing ferrite and pearlite length ratio distributions.

tables.caption: Summary of the tensile tests results obtained before and after hydrogen charging (YS—Yield Strength, TS—Tensile Strength)
